items.title: 2. Crack growth curve
items.text:
Jump to the worked notebook

The external pipe crack tutorial uses a Paris curve to propagate a flaw in a hollow cylinder under a variable axial force.

Use TabulatedGeometryFactor(initial_depth, depths, factors) from py_fatigue.geometry to propagate one crack dimension with get_crack_growth and a table of dimensionless geometry factors. Provide dimensions in the Paris curve's length unit. The solver interpolates the factors linearly and reports geometry_limit at the last tabulated dimension. The MERC-3 tutorial compares this calculation with the handbook's reported crack-growth lives.

Crack growth curve equations have been extensively studied since the '50s of the last century, almost in conjunction with the first catastrophic accident of the first jet transportation aircraft, the De Havilland Comet 1 (1954), where the propagation of fatigue cracks in the upper fuselage panels, starting from the sharp corner of the top rectangular

windows brought 35 deaths. As Frost and Dugdale already pointed out in 1958, the cylindrical specimens were the protagonists of the first half of the 20th century in the panorama of fatigue, and this typology of specimens makes really complex the study of crack growth, meaning that no special attention up to that moment was given to crack growth testing of sheet specimens. Secondly, Frost and Dugdale observed that "In aircraft structures the 'fail-safe' design philosophy requires the structure to be constructed in such a way that fatigue cracks do not cause catastrophic failure before corrective measures can be taken". The first scientist that emphasized the necessity to have polished surfaces to minimize the hotspots from where a crack can propagate is Griffith who extended the theorem of minimum potential energy to the phenomena of rupture of elastic solids. Griffith's work was motivated by Inglis' linear elastic solution for the stress around an elliptical hole asymptotically loaded in tension, from which he predicted that the stress would go to infinite as the ratio between the minor and major axis goes to zero. Griffith's theory provides correct predictions as long as brittle materials, such as glass or ceramics, are considered. Starting from the pioneering work of Griffith, Berto and Lazzarin provided an exhaustive overview of local approaches for the description of brittle and quasi-brittle fracture of engineering materials. Anyway, since in structural materials there is almost always some inelastic deformations around the crack faces, Griffith's hypothesis of linear elastic medium in structural metals application becomes highly unrealistic. For this reason, the first crack growth equation relating the stress with the crack growth rate (i.e. the crack length increment per cycle) did not make use of the elastic energy approach. The formulation dates 1953 and has been proposed by Head; it is based on Inglis' solution and the final simplified form of the crack growth equation is

\[\frac{da}{dN} = \phi \left( \Delta \sigma, \sigma_{Y} , \sigma'_{f} \right) \cdot a^{\frac{3}{2}} \cdot t_{p}^{\frac{3}{2}}\]

Where \(N\) is the number of cycles, \(\phi(\sigma)\) is (asymptotically) a linear function of the stress, yielding, and strength, \(a\) is the half crack size, and \(t_p\) is the thickness of the plastic zone ahead of the crack tip. Frost and Dugdale argued that \(t_p\) is not a constant independent of crack length and derived the exponential model for crack propagation, seldom used up to nowadays

\[\begin{aligned} \frac{da}{dN} &= k_{FD} (\Delta \sigma)^3 a \\ \ln\left(\frac{a}{a_i}\right) &= k_{FD} (\Delta \sigma)^3 N \end{aligned}\]

In which ai is the initial size of the crack and kFD is an experimental quantity depending on the cubic power of the remote stress range \(\Delta \sigma\). During WWII, a group of researchers of the U.S. Naval Research Labs headed by George Rankine Irwin realized that plasticity plays an important role in in fracture mechanics. On this purpose, Griffith's energy formulation was modified in order to make it account for plasticity, too, i.e. the energy release was redefined by adding a plastic dissipation term. Another major achievement of Irwin's work is certainly the relation between the energy release rate \(\hat{G}\) and the stress intensity factor in opening mode \(K_I\):

\[\hat{G} = K_I^2 / E^{\star}\]

where \(E^{\star}=E\) for plain stress or \(E/(1-\nu^2)\) for plane strain. The critical stress intensity factor is the value of \(K\) beyond which a crack starts to propagate and is addressed as fracture toughness \(K_C\). Namely, the toughness is the resistance to fracture of a material, it is a material property and is defined as the stress intensity factor required for a crack to advance from length a to a C. The fracture toughness values have been grouped by material family by Ashby and are shown here below.

Few years later, in 1963, Paris and Erdogan published a work substantiated by many experimental tests where they postulated, differently from Head or Frost and Dugdale, that the crack growth is described by a power law of the stress intensity factor, viz.

\[\frac{da}{dN} = C \left( \Delta K \right)^m\]

At the time of publication, the authors were uncertain on the value of the exponent m, in fact there is a famous statement in their paper saying: "The authors are hesitant but cannot resist the temptation to draw the straight line slope 1/4 through the data...". Therefore, the so-called Paris' law, or Paris-Erdogan law, has been formulated in principle with fixed m=4. Indeed, as evident from the figure here below (from Ashby's book), the majority of engineering alloys is concentrated in the neighborhood of m=4, and this may have tricked the authors.

Paris' law is considered valid within the range \(\Delta K_{th} < \Delta K < \Delta K_{cr}\), where \(\Delta K_{cr}\) is the critical stress intensity factor range which depends on the toughness as \(\Delta K_{cr} = (1-R)K_{Ic}\), with R load ratio, and \(\Delta K_{th}\) is the threshold value below which the crack should not propagate.

items.title: a. Definition of multiple Paris' laws
items.text:
Note

In this example we define four Paris curves for free corrosion as per DNVGL-RP-C203 and plot them using matplotlib and ECharts. We additionally define a random Gaussian stress range-cycles history to plot against the curves defined.

# Paris' laws constants
SIF = np.linspace(1,2500, 300)
SLOPE_1 = np.array([2.88, 8.16])
INTERCEPT_1 = np.array([1.21E-16, 3.98E-29])
SLOPE_2 = np.array([8.16, 2.88])
INTERCEPT_2 = np.array([1.21E-26, 3.98E-13])
SLOPE_3 = 8.16
INTERCEPT_3 = 1.21E-26
THRESHOLD = 75.
CRITICAL = 2000.

# Paris' curves definition
pc_1 = pf.ParisCurve(slope=SLOPE_1, intercept=INTERCEPT_1, norm="The norm",
                    environment="Environment", curve="nr. 1")
pc_2 = pf.ParisCurve(slope=SLOPE_1, intercept=INTERCEPT_1,threshold=THRESHOLD,
                    critical=CRITICAL, norm="The norm",
                    environment="Environment", curve="nr. 2")
pc_3 = pf.ParisCurve(slope=SLOPE_3, intercept=INTERCEPT_3, norm="The norm",
                 environment="Environment", curve="nr. 3")
pc_4 = pf.ParisCurve(slope=SLOPE_2, intercept=INTERCEPT_2,threshold=THRESHOLD,
                    critical=CRITICAL, norm="The norm",
                    environment="Environment", curve="nr. 4")

# Plotting
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(12, 8))
pc_1.plot(fig=fig, ax=axs[0],)
pc_3.plot(fig=fig, ax=axs[0],)
pc_2.plot(fig=fig, ax=axs[1],)
pc_4.plot(fig=fig, ax=axs[1],)
axs[0].legend()
axs[1].legend()
plt.show()

To explore both panels interactively, render the figure in ECharts.

from py_fatigue.plotting import to_echarts

to_echarts(fig).render("paris-curves.html")

items.title: b. Mean stress effect on Paris' law
items.text:
Note

This function has been added from version 1.2.0.

In the following years there have been many attempts to generalize Paris' law, mainly to account for mean stress effect, crack closure and near threshold/near failure modelling. The simplest model of Paris' law for mean stress effect has been proposed in 1970 by Walker:

\[\frac{da}{dN} = C_0 \left( \frac{\Delta K}{(1-R)^{1-\gamma}}\right)^m\]

With \(\gamma\) being Walker exponent, \(R\) the load ratio, and \(C_0\) being the intercept at \(R=0\).

Input:

# Paris's law with Walker correction constants
SLOPE = 4.
INTERCEPT = 1.21E-16
WALKER_EXPONENT = 0.5
LOAD_RATIOS = [0, 0.1, 0.5, 0.7]
THRESHOLDS = 75. * (1 - np.array(LOAD_RATIOS)) ** (1 - WALKER_EXPONENT)
CRITICAL = 2000. * (1 - np.array(LOAD_RATIOS)) ** (1 - WALKER_EXPONENT)

# Walker's curve definition

walker_curves = [pf.WalkerCurve(slope=SLOPE, intercept=INTERCEPT,
                               walker_exponent=WALKER_EXPONENT,
                               threshold=t, critical=c, load_ratio=l,
                               norm="The norm", environment="Environment",
                               curve=f"load_ratio={l}")
                for l, t, c in zip(LOAD_RATIOS, THRESHOLDS, CRITICAL)]

# Plotting
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(6, 4))
for pc in walker_curves:
    pc.plot(fig=fig, ax=ax)
ax.legend()
plt.show()

The effective Paris coefficient at load ratio \(R\) is \(C(R) = C_0 / (1-R)^{m(1-\gamma)}\).

Output:

items.title: c. Paris' law curve interpolation
items.text:
Note

This function has been added from version 1.2.0.

It is now possible to build a piecewise Paris' law curve by interpolating between a set of \"knee points\". The class method :pypyfatigue.crack.ParisCurve.from_knee_points will enforce the piecewise curve to pass through the given points.

Warning

The function does not perform a curve fit, but rather enforces the curve to pass through the given points. Therefore, the number of knee points should be at least equal to the number of segments plus one.

\[\frac{da}{dN} = C \left( \Delta K \right)^m\]

in log-coordinate system, the equation becomes

\[\log \left( \frac{da}{dN} \right) = \log C + m \log \Delta K\]

directly retrieving the well-known linear equation \(Y = M \cdot X + Q\), where \(M=m\) and \(Q=\log C\).

Input:

knee_points = """
   29, 6.93e-14
   30, 8.64e-13
   35, 4.98e-12
   50, 2.50e-11
   72, 1.44e-10
  800, 1.18e-6
1_200, 1.87e-5
1_300, 3.10e-4
"""
# Convert the string data to a list of lists
knee_points_list = [list(map(float, line.split(',')))
                    for line in knee_points.strip().split('\n')]
knee_points_list = np.array(knee_points_list)

c_fkp = pf.ParisCurve.from_knee_points(knee_sif=knee_points_list[:,0],
                                       knee_growth_rate=knee_points_list[:,1],
                                       norm="Simil-NASGRO",
                                       environment="N/A", curve="Interpolated")
# Plotting
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1,1)
c_fkp.plot(fig=fig, ax=ax)
ax.legend(prop={'size': 8})
plt.show()

Output:

Applying the Walker correction to the interpolated curve:

# SLOPE = 4.
# INTERCEPT = 1.21E-16
SLOPES = c_fkp.slope
INTERCEPTS = c_fkp.intercept
THRESHOLD = c_fkp.threshold
CRITICAL = c_fkp.critical
WALKER_EXPONENT = 0.5
LOAD_RATIOS = [0, 0.1, 0.5, 0.7]
THRESHOLDS = THRESHOLD * (1 - np.array(LOAD_RATIOS)) ** (1 - WALKER_EXPONENT)
CRITICALS = CRITICAL * (1 - np.array(LOAD_RATIOS)) ** (1 - WALKER_EXPONENT)

# Walker's curve definition

walker_curves = [pf.WalkerCurve(slope=SLOPES, intercept=INTERCEPTS,
                                walker_exponent=WALKER_EXPONENT,
                                threshold=t, critical=c, load_ratio=l,
                                norm="The norm", environment="Environment",
                                curve=f"load_ratio={l}")
                 for l, t, c in zip(LOAD_RATIOS, THRESHOLDS, CRITICALS)]

# Plotting
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1,1)
for pc in walker_curves:
    pc.plot(fig=fig, ax=ax)
ax.legend(prop={'size': 8})
plt.show()

Output:

items.text:
Jump to the worked notebook

The CycleCount class incorporates the main information about a processed signal for fatigue analysis.

items.title: a. Constant fatigue load
items.text:
Note

In this example we define a fatigue stress signal in the form of a sinusoidal function.

We then feed our signal to the CycleCount class.

Define the time and stress arrays

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from py_fatigue import CycleCount

t = np.arange(0, 10.1, 0.1)  # (in seconds)
s = 200 * np.sin(np.pi*t) + 100   # (in MPa)
plt.plot(t, s)
plt.xlabel("time, s")
plt.ylabel("stress, MPa")
plt.show()

Define the CycleCount instance

cc = CycleCount.from_timeseries(s, t, name="Example")
cc.summary()

Generate a Weibull-distributed stress history and count its cycles.

Define the time and stress arrays

import py_fatigue.testing as test

# Simulate a random signal
t = test.get_sampled_time(duration=10000, fs=10)
s = test.get_random_data(
  t=t, min_=-30, range_=180, random_type="weibull", a=2., seed=42
)
# Plot the signal
plt.plot(t, s, 'k', lw=0.5)

cycle_count = CycleCount.from_timeseries(

items.title: Import measured or generated stress histories
items.text:
SEP005pyExSi

Use CycleCount.from_sep005() with records from an SDyPy reader. One record with one-dimensional data returns a count. A list of records or a record with multiple channel rows returns a flat list in input order. The connector accepts stress in Pa, kPa, MPa, or GPa and returns MPa. An omitted quantity means stress and an omitted unit means Pa.

from py_fatigue import CycleCount

record = {
    "name": "Axial stress",
    "data": [0, 20e6, 3e6, 40e6, 0],
    "fs": 50,
    "quantity": "s",
    "unit_str": "Pa",
}
measured = CycleCount.from_sep005(record)

For a synthetic stress history, install pyExSi separately. Its sine sweep returns a unitless waveform. Here the factor of 20 defines a synthetic stress amplitude in MPa.

import numpy as np
import pyExSi
from py_fatigue import CycleCount

fs = 200
time = np.arange(fs * 20) / fs
stress = 20 * pyExSi.sine_sweep(time, freq_start=2, freq_stop=10)
generated = CycleCount.from_pyexsi(stress, fs=fs, unit="MPa")

SignalForge can also generate nonstationary stress histories. If the generator's signal.x samples already represent stress in MPa, use CycleCount.from_timeseries(signal.x, unit="MPa"). Convert measured or generated acceleration or force into stress using your own model before cycle counting.

Supply either count directly to get_crack_growth(count, paris_curve, geometry) for Paris crack growth with a curve in MPa √mm and dimensions in mm. For ordered NASGRO propagation, supply the tensile extrema and cycle counts as explicit LoadBlock instances.

items.title: 5. Mean stress effect
items.text:
Jump to the worked notebook

Fatigue is cyclic loading fracture. Cyclic loading contain load variation from minimum to maximum and this cycle repeats fornumber of times. When minimum and maximum load is same in magnitude but opposite in direction like tension and compressionor heating and cooling, then mean stress is zero. But when min and maxi load are not identical in magnitude then it contain someamount of residual stress which is called as mean stress. Mean stress affect the fatigue life of component. Generally positive ormean stress in tension has bad effect on component. Its life get reduced as mean stress get increased. But if mean stress is incompression then it increases the life of component

Structural members subjected to in-service cyclic loads exhibit a fatigue behavior that generally depends on the mean stress values. Mean stress is generally taken as average of minimum stress and maximum stress. Mean stress in cyclic loading plays important role. For a given fatigue load range a tensile mean normal stress has a detrimental effect on fatigue strength, whereas, in general, a compressive mean normal stress has a beneficial effect. The problem of the mean stress effect on fatigue life has been approached practically by developing empirical relationships. For metals and alloys, various criteria have been proposed to deal with the mean stress effect on fatigue life.

In [py-fatigue]{.title-ref} the mean stress effect can be compensated by using any of the following models:

  • DNVGL-RP-C203;
  • Walker;
  • Smith-Watson-Topper.

items.title: DNVGL-RP-C203 correction
items.text:
Calculates the mean stress correction according to par. 2.5 of DNVGL-RP-C203, which includes an attenuation factor \(p\) for the stress ranges if the following cases:

  • base material without significant residual stresses \(\rightarrow p = 0.6\). This option neglects fully compressive cycles.
  • welded connections without significant residual stresses \(\rightarrow p = 0.8\). This option multiplies the stress range of fully compressive cycles by p.

Given that the stress ranges are \(\Delta \sigma\), the corrected stress ranges are:

\[\Delta \sigma_{corr} = f_m \cdot \Delta \sigma\]

where:

\[f_m = \frac{\sigma_{max} + p \cdot \vert \sigma_{min} \vert}{\sigma_{max} + \vert\sigma_{min} \vert}\]

with:

\[\frac{\sigma_a}{\vert \sigma_m \vert} \leq 1, \quad \sigma_a = \frac{\sigma_{max} - \sigma_{min}}{2} \,\land \, \sigma_m = \frac{\sigma_{max} + \sigma_{min}}{2}\]

items.title: Walker correction
items.text:
Calculates the mean stress correction according to Walker model.

The correction is given by:

\[\Delta \sigma_{corr} = {\sigma_{max}} ^ {(1 - \gamma)} \, \sigma_{alt} ^ {\gamma}\]

with:

\[\sigma_{max} = \sigma_{mean} + \sigma_{alt}\]

items.title: Smith-Watson-Topper
items.text:
Calculates the mean stress correction according to Smith-Watson-Topper model. It is equivalent to the Walker model with gamma = 0.5.

The correction is given by:

\[\Delta \sigma_{corr} = \sqrt{\sigma_{max} \, \sigma_{alt}}\]

with:

\[\sigma_{max} = \sigma_{mean} + \sigma_{alt}\]

items.title: 6. Stress-Life damage calculation
items.text:
Jump to the worked notebook

This section contains some examples of damage calculations using the stress-life approach.

The tube in bending tutorial starts with a tube section and a moment history, then connects rainflow counting, mean-stress correction and equivalent loads to Miner damage.

The module py_fatigue.damage.stress_life contains all the damage models related to the stress-life approach.

The simplest and most common damage model is the Palmgren-Miner (py_fatigue.damage.stress_life.calc_pm, py_fatigue.damage.stress_life.get_pm) model.

\[D = \sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{blocks}}} \frac{n_j}{N_j} \leq 1\]

Besides the linear damage accumulation rule, [py-fatigue]{.title-ref} also provides a series of nonlinear damage accumulation models callable through py_fatigue.damage.stress_life.calc_nonlinear_damage and py_fatigue.damage.stress_life.get_nonlinear_damage

  • Manson and Halford
  • Si Jian et al.
  • Pavlou
  • Leve

The generic form of a nonlinear damage rule is:

\[D = \left( \left( \dots \left( \left( \left(\frac{n_1}{N_1}\right)^{e_{1, 2}} + \frac{n_2}{N_2} \right)^{e_{2, 3}} + \frac{n_3}{N_3} \right)^{e_{3, 4}} + \dots + \frac{n_{M-1}}{N_{M-1}} \right)^{e_{M-1, M}} + \dots + \frac{n_M}{N_M} \right)^{e_M}\]

where \(n_j\) is the number of cycles in the fatigue histogram at the \(j\)-th cycle, \(N_j\) is the number of cycles to failure at the \(j\)-th cycle, \(e_{j, j+1}\) is the exponent for the \(j\)-th and \(j+1\)-th cycles, \(M\) is the number of load blocks in the fatigue spectrum.

The formula is conveniently rewritten as pseudocode:

# retrieve N_j using the fatigue histogram and SN curve
# retrieve the exponents e_{j, j+1}
#  calculate the damage
D = 0
for j in range(1, M+1):
    D = (D + n_j / N_j) ^ e_{j, j+1}

Specifically, for the damage models currently implemented in [py_fatigue]{.title-ref}, the exponents are:

  • Manson and Halford: \(e_{j, j+1} = \left(\frac{N_{j}}{N_{j+1}}\right)^{\alpha}\) with \(\alpha=0.4\) usually.
  • Si Jian et al.: \(e_{j, j+1} = \sigma_{j+1} / \sigma_{j}\) where \(\sigma_{j+1}\) is the stress amplitude for the \(j\)-th cycle.
  • Pavlou: \(e_{j, j+1} = \left(\frac{\Delta \sigma_j / 2}{\sigma_U}\right)^{\alpha}\) where \(\Delta \sigma_j/2\) is the stress amplitude, \(\sigma_U\) is the ultimate stress, \(\Delta \sigma\) is the stress range and \(\alpha=0.75\) (usually) is the exponent.
  • Leve: \(e_{j, j+1} =\text{constant}\).

items.title: 7. Ordered plate crack propagation
items.text:
Jump to the worked notebook

The plate crack tutorial follows a through crack and a surface crack from their initial profiles to their final dimensions, using a NASGRO material fit and the same tensile load history for both cases.

Open lesson 33 to compare both plate geometries using the same ordered load blocks. The plots align applied stress, crack dimensions, and peak stress intensity on cumulative cycles. To edit and rerun it locally, use uv run marimo edit notebooks/33-ordered_crack_growth.py.

Open lesson 34 to generate a long tensile waveform and follow it to a Miner damage limit and a crack-growth toughness stop.

Use the family notebooks to run ordered crack propagation and overlay the initial and last accepted profiles. Through cracks · lesson 35 · Surface cracks · lesson 36

items.title: What each new name does
items.text:
The following API is experimental in this release candidate. Each operation can be learned independently before running a propagation analysis.

Name Inputs and output CenterThroughCrack(half_width, half_length) TC01 symmetric center crack. Its stress_intensity(stress) method returns one opening-mode intensity. Both dimensions are half-dimensions. EdgeThroughCrack(width, length) TC02 single edge crack. Give the full plate width and the distance from the edge to the tip. Its stress_intensity(stress) method returns one opening-mode intensity. SphereThroughCrack(mean_radius, thickness, half_length) TC06 through-wall arc on a great circle. The half-length follows the mid-wall arc. AxialCylinderThroughCrack(mean_radius, thickness, half_length) TC07 longitudinal through-wall crack. Use hoop membrane stress to open the crack. CircumferentialCylinderThroughCrack(mean_radius, thickness, half_length, length, poisson) TC08 through-wall arc in a thin cylinder. The half-length follows the mid-wall arc and length is the full axial cylinder length. Use axial membrane stress. SemiEllipticalSurfaceCrack(half_width, thickness, depth, half_length) SC01 surface crack. Its stress_intensity(stress) method returns a pair ordered as deepest point, free surface. CircumferentialCylinderSurfaceCrack(inner_radius, thickness, depth, half_length) SC05 external pipe crack under axial tension. half_length follows the outer-surface arc. Intensities are ordered as deepest point, free surface. RoundBarSurfaceCrack(diameter, depth) SC07 circular surface crack in a solid bar. Its stress_intensity(stress) method returns one deepest-point intensity for remote tension. RolledBoltThreadSurfaceCrack(major_diameter, minor_diameter, depth) SC08 thumbnail in a rolled thread. The single intensity is at the deepest point. HoleBoreSurfaceCrack(width, thickness, hole_diameter, depth, half_length, crack_count) SC11 one or two symmetric cracks at a plate hole. Give the full plate dimensions. Intensities are ordered as radial tip, bore tip. NasgroCurve Stores calibrated material inputs. get_growth_rate(length, k_min, k_max) evaluates one growth rate in mm/cycle at a crack-front point. This is a material calculation without integration. LoadBlock(minimum, maximum, cycles) Represents repeated loading between two stress extrema. A sequence of blocks preserves the applied order. simulate_crack_growth(geometry, curve, loads, ...) Combines the geometry, NASGRO material law, and ordered loads to advance the crack over time. GrowthResult and GrowthPoint The result contains accepted points and a termination reason. A point records cycles, crack dimensions, per-tip intensities, and the zero-based block index.

Open the plate intensity example or open the NASGRO rate example to see these operations on their own.

items.title: Plate solutions and loads
items.text: The ordered solver uses tensile membrane loads. TC01 uses the finite-width secant solution, TC02 uses Tada's single-edge tension equation for lengths through 0.8 of the plate width, and SC01 uses the Newman–Raju finite-width surface-crack tension solution. TC02 was checked against a published uniform-tension strip benchmark. Tada equation and loading conventions · NASA strip benchmark, Table 3 · Newman–Raju surface crack

items.title: Through cracks in thin shells
items.text:
TC06 and TC07 use the FLAGRO 2.0 expressions reproduced in NASA CR-4706, with half_length / sqrt(mean_radius * thickness) limited to 3 and 10, respectively. The inputs to stress_intensity() and LoadBlock are opening membrane stresses in MPa. If starting from pressure p, use p * mean_radius / (2 * thickness) for TC06 and p * mean_radius / thickness for TC07. NASA CR-4706, TC06 · NASA CR-4706, TC07

TC08 uses the Forman–Sanders solution for axial membrane tension. The supported domain requires a total arc angle below 270°, an axial length of at least 2 * mean_radius * sqrt(mean_radius / thickness), and a mean radius at least ten times the wall thickness. The last restriction keeps the implementation in the thin-shell range used for comparison. The bending component and net-section stress for the shell models remain outside this implementation. NASFLA geometry, Fig. 2.2.6 · Rege, Table 8.2

items.title: Surface cracks in pipes, bars, threads and plate holes
items.text:
SC05 uses the external-crack, axial-tension factors from Raju and Newman's Table 1, with linear interpolation along each table axis. Supply gross-section axial stress in MPa. With pipe inner radius R, thickness t, radial depth a and outer arc half-length c, the table spans 1 ≤ R/t ≤ 10, 0.2 ≤ a/t ≤ 0.8, and 0.6 ≤ a/c ≤ 1. NASA TM-87594, Table 1

SC07 uses the Forman–Shivakumar round-bar tension factor for 0 < depth < diameter / 2. The solver advances the deepest point and the plot constructs the circular front from depth. This case supports remote tension. Bending and the Appendix B net-section calculation remain outside this implementation. Handbook, Table 11.3.13 · NASFLA Fig. 2.2.52

SC08 covers a thumbnail at first contact in a rolled aerospace bolt thread. Use S₀ = 4F/(πd²) in MPa, where F is the applied axial force in N and d is the minor diameter in mm. Supply the actual tensile extrema, including any known preload. The deepest tip uses K = S₀ F₀ √(πa), with the a/c = 1 column of Table 2 interpolated linearly over 0 < a/d ≤ 0.5. Fig. 2 identifies d as the reference diameter for this branch. The thread cross section is a schematic that preserves the radial depth and surface arc length. Mettu et al., NLR-TP-99313, §5, Table 2 and Fig. 2

SC11 uses Newman and Raju's finite-width tension equations for a centered hole and either one crack or two identical cracks, both at the plate mid-plane. Supply gross-section remote tensile stress in MPa. The public depth is the radial distance into the ligament and half_length is the half-length along the bore. The source calls these c and a, respectively. The fit requires 0.2 ≤ half_length/depth ≤ 2, half_length < thickness/2, 0.5 ≤ hole_diameter/thickness ≤ 2 and (hole_diameter + 2·depth)/width < 0.5. NASA TM-85793, Eqs. 53–64 and Table 1

These additions cover axial or remote tension. Internal SC05 cracks, machined SC08 threads, SC11 pin bearing, and bending need their own load and geometry treatments. Growth stops when the crack leaves the supported domain. The last accepted profile is available without a through-crack transition.

items.title: Net-section stress
items.text: For TC01, TC02 and SC01, geometry.net_section_stress(stress) returns the Appendix B net-section stress in MPa under the supplied nonnegative membrane stress. TC02 and SC01 include bending caused by the shift in the net-section centroid. This method reports a diagnostic. The propagation solver evaluates stress intensity from the applied gross-section stress and the geometry solution. The Appendix B yield and flow checks require separate material inputs.

items.title: Plot the geometry, material law and result
items.text:
Call geometry.plot() or geometry.echarts() to draw the initial plate crack. Pass result=result to overlay the last accepted profile. Surface cracks are drawn in the crack plane of the plate, pipe, bar, or thread. If a run stops before accepting a state, the plot shows the starting geometry.

fig, ax = geometry.plot(result=result)
geometry.echarts(result=result)

Call curve.plot() or curve.echarts() to show the long-crack reference curve at stress ratio R = 0 (k_min = 0). Both sweep maximum stress intensity up to toughness and mark that limit with a dashed line. Supply length to apply the finite-crack correction to the growth threshold and k_min to change the minimum stress intensity.

fig, ax = curve.plot()
curve.echarts()

fig, ax = curve.plot(length=4.0, k_min=20.0, scale="loglog")

fig, ax = result.plot()
result.echarts()

A scalar k_max sets a shorter sweep endpoint. Supply an array to evaluate exact sample points, or a one-element array to show one point. With explicit samples, k_min can be one value or an array paired with k_max. Use scale="semilogx" to show zero growth below threshold, or scale="semilogy" for the default logarithmic growth-rate axis.

To compare results on shared axes, use other_result.plot(ax=ax, label="Surface crack"). The plot uses the accepted points in result.history.

items.title: Material inputs
items.text:
coefficient and exponent set the scale and power of the growth law. The coefficient depends on the units and the exponent. threshold_zero is the long-crack threshold at stress ratio zero. threshold_fanning controls how the threshold changes with stress ratio. p controls the threshold term, which is disabled at p = 0. toughness is the critical maximum stress intensity. q controls the near-toughness term. The solver's toughness stop still applies at q = 0. constraint and peak_to_flow parameterize the crack-opening law. Both stay fixed for the current run.

The pointwise rate method requires a positive crack length and 0 ≤ k_min < k_max < toughness. The propagation solver handles a zero-range block and checks toughness before evaluating the rate.

items.title: Solver controls and result
items.text:
The current solver requires four controls. max_cycle_step caps a single integration step in cycles. length_tolerance controls the absolute difference in mm between one full step and two half steps. cycle_tolerance controls the terminal bracket width in cycles. max_trials is an implementation limit that counts accepted and rejected trials. Exhausting it raises an error. Its design is under review.

termination identifies spectrum exhaustion, a toughness stop, or a geometry limit. final_cycles reports the last accepted cycle count, or zero if no state was accepted. At a stop inside a step, it reports the admissible side of the bracket. Treat the output accordingly when comparing against a reference life.

Use simulate_crack_growth for an ordered sequence of tensile membrane load blocks. Each block carries a minimum stress, a maximum stress, and a fractional cycle count. Preserve the order in which the blocks occur. A binned cycle count does not establish that order.

The plate geometries use crack dimensions and plate dimensions in mm. Use MPa for applied stresses and MPa √mm for stress intensity. A center crack takes crack and plate half-widths. A surface crack takes depth and half-length and returns intensities at the deepest point and the free surface in that order.

The implemented center-crack range is \(0 < a/b \le 0.8\), and the surface fit uses \(0 < a/c \le 1.2\), \(0 < a/t \le 0.8\), and \(0 < c/b < 0.5\). For surface cracks deeper than their half-length, SC01 uses the companion Newman–Raju fit in NASA TM-83200. The solution uses linear-elastic stress intensity in uniform membrane tension. The solver stops at a toughness or geometry limit. Its final point is the last accepted state on the admissible side of the terminal cycle bracket.

NasgroCurve uses the NASGRO 3.0 growth and threshold equations with a fixed, user-supplied toughness and the Newman opening law at nonnegative stress ratios. For SC01 growth at the free surface, the solver scales \(\Delta K\) by \(\beta_R=0.9+0.2R^2-0.1R^4\). Intensity plots, history and the toughness check use the applied intensities. SwRI release notes, pp. 5–6

Supply calibrated material inputs in the stated unit system. Bending, retardation, geometry transitions, and the NASGRO material database are outside this implementation.

The TC01 regression reproduces the published 7075-T6 constant-amplitude life within 0.3% using the rounded inputs in Figures 5 and 8. The SC01 regression checks the crack shape at several depths against the published 2219-T87 tension prediction. It also reproduces the NASA/FLAGRO specimen 5576 pre-breakthrough depth history within 0.01 in at four cycle counts through 40,000 cycles. That comparison uses the reported Walker law at fixed stress ratio. Exact version-specific NASFLA agreement requires a matching input deck and output history.

  • Center crack finite-width solution
  • TC01 life reference
  • Newman–Raju surface crack fit and growth shape, Figure 12
  • Deep surface crack fit, equations 16–25
  • SC01 depth history, NASA TM-100383, pp. 15–17
  • NASGRO 3.0 rate and threshold equations
  • Newman opening law

See the ordered crack-growth API reference for signatures and source code.

items.title: Count cycles and calculate Miner damage with MCP
items.text: In this example, use a short stress history to check your MCP connection, then save the individual damage contributions as a CSV. The example S–N curve is illustrative.

items.title: Prepare the input
items.text:
Follow the MCP setup guide and configure both CSV directories. Save this file as stress.csv inside the input directory. Its values are stress samples in MPa, in the order they were measured.

stress
0
75
-15
50
0
path: Count cycles and calculate Miner damage with MCP

items.title: Count the cycles
items.text:
In Codex or another connected client, enter this prompt.

Use the py-fatigue rainflow_count tool with the configured input file
stress.csv. Report the number of cycle rows, total cycle weight, and
stress range of each row.

A client that accepts direct tool arguments can send this to rainflow_count.

{"stress": {"csv_path": "stress.csv"}}

You should get four rows with ranges of 75, 90, 65, and 50 MPa, in that order. Each is a half cycle, so the total cycle weight is 2.
path: Count cycles and calculate Miner damage with MCP

items.title: Calculate and export the damage
items.text:
Ask the client to run miner_damage on the same file using slope 3 and a log10 intercept of 12, and to export the full contribution table. You can also pass these arguments directly.

{
  "source": {
    "kind": "stress_history",
    "stress": {"csv_path": "stress.csv"}
  },
  "curve": {"slope": 3, "intercept": 12},
  "export_csv": true
}

The total damage is approximately 7.7525e-7. Open the generated file under the configured output directory using the relative path in the tool result. The file contains four data rows and columns for the stress range, cycle weight, and damage contribution.

For larger inputs, the preview shows up to five rows and the total uses the entire history. See the ordered crack-growth example for a separate workflow based on load blocks in their applied order.
